learningObjective: Precisely characterize partial evaluation and identify a canonical use case.

canonicalClaims.claim: Partial evaluation specializes a program p(s, d) with respect to static input s, producing a residual program p_s(d) that behaves equivalently to p(s, d) for all d; constant folding, template specialization, and shape specialization are instances.
conditions: The partition of inputs into static and dynamic is well-defined.
Semantics preservation: residual program equals original for all dynamic inputs given the fixed static inputs.
nonImplications: Does not imply the residual program is always faster or smaller; specialization can increase code size.
Does not imply partial evaluation is always applicable; some computations depend on d in ways that resist specialization.

misconceptions.claim: Partial evaluation is the same as lazy evaluation.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Lazy evaluation defers computation until a value is needed at runtime; partial evaluation performs computation at specialization/compile time.
misconceptions.sourceOrEvidence: Jones, Gomard, Sestoft — Partial Evaluation textbook

misconceptions.claim: Partial evaluation is a peephole optimization.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Peephole is a local backend optimization on a small instruction window; partial evaluation specializes whole subprograms with respect to static inputs.

misconceptions.claim: Partial evaluation only works with constant inputs.
misconceptions.whyWrong: It applies to any known-at-specialization input, including partial data structures, shapes, and types.

implementationFacts: Futamura's first projection: partially evaluating an interpreter with respect to a source program yields a compiled program.
TorchDynamo/TorchInductor specialize on tensor shapes at compile time (a form of partial evaluation).
C++ template instantiation is a limited compile-time PE.
performanceScenarios: Shape specialization in ML compilers trades compile time and cache footprint for faster kernel dispatch.
